title: The Spanish Empire
description: An illustrated world map of how Spain’s crowns built the first empire on which the sun never set, from the fall of Granada and Columbus’s voyage in 1492, through the conquest of the Aztec and Inca states, silver and the Manila galleons, to independence in the Americas and the last colony in Africa in 1976.
mapLabel: Illustrated world map of the Spanish Empire and its rivals from 1492 to 1976
note: Based on standard histories of the period. The map is stylised and not to scale: it uses a simple flat projection, so lands far from the equator look larger than they are. The empires under Powers are painted loosely on today’s coastlines, with small holdings shown as dots; many frontiers were claimed rather than ruled. A few close places (Palos, Seville, Cádiz and Granada; Tordesillas and Madrid; Lima, Cusco and Ayacucho; Tenochtitlan and Dolores) have dots that touch. The Manila galleons crossed the Pacific from Acapulco; the map shows only their last leg, from Guam. Place names are those of the time. Deaths from conquest, epidemics, forced labour and war are estimates, and historians differ widely on many of them. Coastlines: Natural Earth.

steps.title: The fall of Granada
steps.text: On 2 January 1492 Muhammad XII (Boabdil), the last Nasrid sultan, hands Granada to Isabella of Castile and Ferdinand of Aragon after a ten-year war. It ends Muslim rule in Iberia, begun in 711. Within months the monarchs order Spain’s Jews to convert or leave, and agree to back a Genoese sailor’s plan to reach Asia by sailing west.
steps.today: Today: Granada, Andalusia, Spain; the Alhambra palace still stands.

steps.title: Landfall in the Bahamas
steps.text: Columbus sails from Palos on 3 August 1492 with three ships, the Santa María, Pinta and Niña, and calls at the Canary Islands. On 12 October his crew sight an island the Lucayan Taíno call Guanahani; he names it San Salvador. Which island it was is disputed. He goes on to Cuba and Hispaniola, convinced he has reached Asia.
steps.today: Today: probably San Salvador Island, the Bahamas; other islands are proposed.

steps.title: A line across the world
steps.text: Portugal protests that the new lands fall in its sphere. After papal rulings in 1493, the two crowns meet at Tordesillas and draw a line 370 leagues west of the Cape Verde Islands: lands to its west for Castile, to its east for Portugal. The line later gives Portugal Brazil. No one asks the peoples who live there.
steps.today: Today: Tordesillas, Castile and León, Spain.

steps.title: The first colony
steps.text: On Columbus’s second voyage settlers found Isabela on Hispaniola, then Santo Domingo, about 1496, Spain’s first lasting city in the Americas. Taíno people are forced to dig gold and farm for settlers under grants of their labour (encomienda). War, overwork, hunger and later smallpox destroy them: within decades few remain, though how many lived there before is disputed.
steps.today: Today: Santo Domingo, capital of the Dominican Republic.

steps.title: The fall of Tenochtitlan
steps.text: Hernán Cortés sails from Cuba in 1519 with about 500 men, and reaches Tenochtitlan with tens of thousands of Indigenous allies, above all from Tlaxcala, who resent Mexica rule. Moctezuma II dies in Spanish custody in 1520. After smallpox sweeps the city, a siege ends with its fall on 13 August 1521. Mexico City is built on its ruins.
steps.today: Today: the centre of Mexico City; the Templo Mayor ruins lie beside the cathedral.

steps.title: Round the world
steps.text: Ferdinand Magellan, a Portuguese captain in Spanish service, leaves Sanlúcar in 1519 with five ships to reach the Spice Islands westwards. In 1520 he finds this strait into the Pacific. He is killed in the Philippines in 1521. Juan Sebastián Elcano brings one ship, the Victoria, home in 1522 with 18 men: the first voyage round the world.
steps.today: Today: the Strait of Magellan, southern Chile.

steps.title: Atahualpa taken
steps.text: Francisco Pizarro sails from Panama and lands in an Inca empire torn by civil war between two brothers, Atahualpa and Huáscar, and already struck by smallpox. At Cajamarca on 16 November 1532 fewer than 200 Spaniards ambush Atahualpa’s largely unarmed retinue; accounts say thousands die. Atahualpa fills a room with gold and silver as ransom, but is executed in 1533.
steps.today: Today: Cajamarca, northern Peru.

steps.title: The Inca capital falls
steps.text: The Spanish enter Cusco in November 1533 and crown Manco Inca as a puppet. In 1536 he rises against them and besieges the city for months, then withdraws to Vilcabamba in the forest, where an Inca state holds out for 36 years. In 1572 a Spanish force takes it, and the last Inca, Túpac Amaru, is beheaded in Cusco’s square.
steps.today: Today: Cusco, Peru; Spanish churches stand on Inca walls.

steps.title: City of the Kings
steps.text: Pizarro founds Lima in 1535, and is murdered there by rivals in 1541. It becomes the seat of the Viceroyalty of Peru, created in 1542. That year the New Laws limit encomiendas and forbid enslaving Indigenous people. Settlers rise under Gonzalo Pizarro, Francisco’s brother, and kill the first viceroy. The crown wins in 1548, but softens the laws.
steps.today: Today: Lima, capital of Peru.

steps.title: The silver mountain
steps.text: In 1545 silver is found in a mountain high in the Andes, and Potosí becomes one of the largest cities in the Americas. From the 1570s Viceroy Francisco de Toledo enforces a rotating draft of forced Indigenous labour (mita) in the mines, where many die. With Zacatecas in Mexico, Potosí makes Spanish America the world’s main source of silver.
steps.today: Today: Potosí, Bolivia; the Cerro Rico is still mined.

steps.title: The treasure fleets
steps.text: From 1503 the House of Trade in Seville controls all trade with the Americas. Convoys (flotas) gather at Havana and sail home each year guarded by warships, laden with silver. The silver pays for Spain’s wars in Europe and flows on to foreign bankers, and through trade to China. Even so, the crown goes bankrupt several times.
steps.today: Today: Seville, Andalusia; the Archive of the Indies keeps the empire’s records.

steps.title: Across the Pacific
steps.text: Miguel López de Legazpi sails from Mexico in 1564 and claims the islands named after Philip II; Andrés de Urdaneta finds a route back east in 1565. Legazpi founds Manila in 1571. For 250 years the Manila galleons carry American silver across the Pacific from Acapulco and bring back Chinese silk and porcelain, linking trade round the world.
steps.today: Today: Manila, capital of the Philippines.

steps.title: Two crowns, one king
steps.text: Philip II, son of Charles V, rules Spain, the Americas, Milan, Naples and the Netherlands. When Portugal’s king dies without an heir, Philip claims the throne and his army takes Lisbon in 1580. Portugal keeps its own laws and empire, but now shares Spain’s king and Spain’s enemies. In 1640 the Portuguese rebel and crown a king of their own.
steps.today: Today: Lisbon, capital of Portugal.

steps.title: The Armada
steps.text: To end English raids and English help for the Dutch rebels, Philip sends a fleet of about 130 ships from Lisbon in 1588 to escort an army from Flanders to England. The English attack it with fireships off Calais and fight it at Gravelines. Driven north round Scotland and Ireland, it loses many ships to storms. The invasion never happens.
steps.today: Today: Gravelines, northern France.

steps.title: The Dutch break away
steps.text: Heavy taxes and the persecution of Protestants drive the Netherlands to revolt in 1568. The southern provinces return to Spanish rule, but the northern seven form a republic that builds its own trading empire, taking Spanish and Portuguese posts in Asia, Africa and the Americas. After eighty years of war, Spain recognises Dutch independence in the Peace of Münster, 1648.
steps.today: Today: Münster, Germany.

steps.title: A new dynasty
steps.text: Charles II, the last Spanish Habsburg, dies childless in 1700 and leaves his crowns to Philip of Anjou, grandson of Louis XIV of France. A European war follows. The peace of Utrecht, 1713, keeps Philip V on the throne and the Americas Spanish, but gives away the Netherlands and Italian lands, and Gibraltar and Minorca to Britain.
steps.today: Today: Madrid, capital of Spain since 1561.

steps.title: Missions to California
steps.text: Bourbon kings tighten their hold on the empire with new viceroyalties, officials and taxes. Fearing Russian and British advances, Spain sends soldiers and Franciscan friars north. Junípero Serra founds the mission of San Diego in 1769, the first of 21 along the coast of Alta California. The missions convert Indigenous people, often by force, and disease devastates them.
steps.today: Today: San Diego, California, United States.

steps.title: The great rebellion
steps.text: In November 1780 José Gabriel Condorcanqui, a chief descended from the Inca, takes the name Túpac Amaru II and leads an uprising against forced labour and new taxes that spreads across the Andes. He is captured and executed in Cusco in May 1781, but fighting goes on until 1783. Estimates of the dead reach 100,000 and are disputed.
steps.today: Today: Cusco, Peru.

steps.title: A constitution under siege
steps.text: In 1808 Napoleon forces the Spanish king to give up his throne and puts his brother Joseph in his place. Spain rises in revolt. While French armies besiege Cádiz, a parliament (Cortes) meets there with delegates from the Americas and in 1812 passes a liberal constitution. In the Americas, local juntas refuse to obey Joseph and begin to rule themselves.
steps.today: Today: Cádiz, Andalusia, Spain.

steps.title: The cry of Dolores
steps.text: On 16 September 1810 Miguel Hidalgo, a parish priest, calls his congregation at Dolores to rise. A vast, poorly armed army follows him; he is captured and shot in 1811, and José María Morelos fights on until his execution in 1815. In 1821 Agustín de Iturbide, a royalist officer, changes sides, and Mexico becomes independent.
steps.today: Today: Dolores Hidalgo, Guanajuato, Mexico.

steps.title: The last battle
steps.text: Simón Bolívar’s armies free Venezuela, Colombia and Ecuador, while José de San Martín crosses the Andes from Argentina to free Chile and enter Lima. At Ayacucho on 9 December 1824, Antonio José de Sucre defeats the last royalist army in South America. By 1826 Spain holds nothing on the American mainland; Cuba and Puerto Rico remain.
steps.today: Today: Ayacucho region, Peru.

steps.title: The disaster of 1898
steps.text: Cubans fight long wars for independence from 1868. In 1898 the American warship Maine explodes in Havana harbour, and the United States declares war. In months Spain’s fleets are sunk at Manila Bay and Santiago de Cuba. The Treaty of Paris hands Puerto Rico, Guam and the Philippines to the United States; Cuba becomes independent under American occupation.
steps.today: Today: Havana, capital of Cuba.

steps.title: War in the Rif
steps.text: In 1912 Spain takes a protectorate over northern Morocco. Rif Berbers led by Abd el-Krim rout a Spanish army at Annual in 1921; estimates of the Spanish dead, from about 8,000 to over 10,000, are disputed. With French help and poison gas, Spain wins by 1927. In 1936 Franco’s Army of Africa crosses from Morocco to fight the Civil War.
steps.today: Today: the Rif, northern Morocco.

steps.title: The last colony
steps.text: Spain gives up its Moroccan protectorate in 1956, and Equatorial Guinea becomes independent in 1968. In November 1975, as Franco lies dying, Morocco sends 350,000 people on the Green March into Spanish Sahara. Spain hands the territory to Morocco and Mauritania and leaves in February 1976. Its status is still disputed. Ceuta, Melilla and the Canary Islands remain Spanish.
steps.today: Today: Laayoune, Western Sahara, a territory whose status is disputed.

items.role: The first great empire in the Americas, built on conquest and silver, with the Philippines as its outpost in Asia. It loses its American mainland by 1826 and its last islands in 1898.

items.name: Isabella I
items.text: Isabella wins Castile in a civil war, and her marriage to Ferdinand of Aragon in 1469 joins Spain’s two main crowns. Together they conquer Granada, expel the Jews, set up the Spanish Inquisition and back Columbus. Their grandson Charles inherits it all.

items.name: Christopher Columbus
items.text: Born in Genoa, Columbus spends years seeking backing for a western route to Asia, based on too small an estimate of the Earth. He makes four voyages from 1492 to 1504. As governor of Hispaniola he rules so harshly that he is sent home in chains in 1500. He dies in Spain in 1506.

items.name: Bartolomé de las Casas
items.role: Dominican friar and Bishop of Chiapas
items.text: A settler and slaveholder on Hispaniola and Cuba, Las Casas gives up his Indigenous labourers in 1514 and spends fifty years denouncing the conquest. His campaigning helps bring about the New Laws of 1542. At Valladolid in 1550 he argues that the peoples of the Americas have rights Spain must respect.

items.name: Charles V
items.role: King of Spain 1516 to 1556, Holy Roman Emperor
items.text: Grandson of Isabella and Ferdinand and of the Emperor Maximilian, Charles inherits Spain and its Americas, the Netherlands, Austria and southern Italy, and is elected emperor in 1519. His reign sees the conquest of Mexico and Peru, and endless war with France, the Ottomans and Protestant princes. Exhausted, he abdicates in 1556.

items.name: Moctezuma II
items.text: Ruler of Tenochtitlan at its height, Moctezuma receives Cortés in 1519 and is soon held captive in his own palace. He dies in 1520 during fighting in the city; Spanish accounts say his own people stoned him, while Indigenous accounts blame the Spanish.

items.name: Hernán Cortés
items.text: A settler in Cuba, Cortés defies its governor to lead the 1519 expedition to Mexico. He wins allies among the Mexica’s enemies and, with the interpreter Malintzin, out-talks and out-fights his rivals. Made governor of New Spain, he is soon sidelined by the crown, and dies in Spain in 1547.

items.name: Malintzin
items.role: interpreter to Cortés, also called La Malinche or Doña Marina
items.text: A Nahua woman sold into slavery and given to Cortés in 1519, she speaks Nahuatl and Maya and soon learns Spanish. As his interpreter and adviser she is central to the conquest. She bears Cortés a son, Martín. In Mexico she has been seen as a traitor, a victim and a mother of the nation.

items.name: Atahualpa
items.text: Son of the emperor Huayna Capac, Atahualpa wins a civil war against his half-brother Huáscar just as Pizarro arrives. Captured at Cajamarca, he has Huáscar killed from captivity. The Spanish take his ransom and then garrotte him in July 1533.

items.name: Francisco Pizarro
items.text: Born in Trujillo in Extremadura, Pizarro serves in Panama before leading three voyages south. With his brothers he conquers the Inca, founds Lima and grows immensely rich. A quarrel over the spoils leads to war with his partner Diego de Almagro, whom he has executed; Almagro’s followers kill Pizarro in Lima in 1541.

items.name: Philip II
items.role: King of Spain from 1556, of Portugal from 1580
items.text: Charles’s son rules from Madrid and his palace of El Escorial, reading reports from across the world. He adds Portugal in 1580, and the Philippines are named after him. He fights the Ottomans, the Dutch, England and France, defends Catholicism fiercely, and leaves his kingdom deep in debt.

items.name: Túpac Amaru II
items.text: José Gabriel Condorcanqui, a mule-train owner and local chief, claims descent from the last Inca. After years of petitioning against forced labour, he seizes and hangs a royal official in 1780 and raises the Andes. Captured, he is executed in Cusco with his wife, Micaela Bastidas, and family members in 1781.

items.name: Miguel Hidalgo
items.role: priest who began Mexico’s war of independence
items.text: A well-read parish priest who teaches his parishioners crafts and trades, Hidalgo joins a conspiracy against Spanish rule. When it is discovered he calls the rising early, in 1810. His army takes Guanajuato but falls apart near Mexico City. Captured, he is shot in Chihuahua in 1811. Mexicans call him the father of the nation.

items.name: Simón Bolívar
items.text: Born to a rich Caracas family, Bolívar leads wars that free Venezuela, Colombia, Ecuador, Peru and Bolivia, which is named after him. He dreams of a united Gran Colombia, but it breaks apart amid rivalries. Ill and disillusioned, he dies in 1830 on his way into exile.
